title: Gulf States Pressure Trump to Halt Iran Strikes as Hormuz Diplomacy Gains Traction
excerpt: Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the UAE urged the U.S. president to pause military action as Qatari mediators present a fresh proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, drawing a cautiously positive response from Tehran.
body:
• Trump called off a planned military strike on Iran after direct appeals from Saudi, Qatari, and Emirati leaders urging more time for diplomacy.
  • Qatari mediators presented Tehran with a fresh proposal to create new shipping traffic patterns through the Strait of Hormuz, which Iran received positively.
  • Gulf states are divided — Saudi Arabia favors de-escalation while the UAE has lobbied for more decisive U.S. action against Iran's Revolutionary Guard Corps.
  • The conflict has driven Brent crude up 24% in a month and threatens Republican prospects in November's midterm elections.

President Donald Trump cancelled a planned military strike on Iran over the weekend after leaders of three Gulf states — Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and the United Arab Emirates — urged the U.S. to allow more time for diplomacy, according to people familiar with the matter and Trump's own statements on Truth Social.

"Based on this request, I have agreed, for the future benefit of the WORLD and, likewise, the survival of a successful and prosperous Iran, to cancel the attack, subject to being able to rapidly make a DEAL," Trump wrote on Saturday. He added that Israel "joins me in this commitment."

Fresh Hormuz Proposal Raises Cautious Hopes

The pause in hostilities came as Qatari mediators presented Iran on Saturday with a fresh proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz, the strategic waterway that carried roughly 20% of the world's oil and liquefied natural gas trade before the war. Iranian diplomats reacted positively to the plan, which would create new traffic patterns for ships transiting the strait, according to the Wall Street Journal.

https://x.com/GuntherEagleman/status/2084221660677177431

Iran's Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi told state news agency IRNA that negotiations between Tehran and Oman over the strait were in their "final stages." However, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said the talks focused on agreeing a new shipping route and had "no link to the Strait of Hormuz being opened or closed."

A key sticking point remains Iran's desire to collect tolls or fees from vessels passing through the strait — a position the U.S. has strongly opposed. Iran also insists on controlling at least part of both shipping lanes, which are bordered by Iran to the north and Oman to the south.

"Everyone knows what will happen if [Iranian] infrastructure will be attacked — they will attack infrastructure in the Gulf states. They created the understanding that there is a huge price to pay."

— Danny Citrinowicz, former Israeli military intelligence official and researcher at the Institute for National Security Studies

Gulf Allies Divided on Strategy

Behind the diplomatic front, Gulf states are far from unified. Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman held a call with Trump hours before the announcement, stressing "the necessity of prioritising dialogue to de-escalate tensions," according to Saudi state media. The kingdom has consistently favored de-escalation, even previously blocking a U.S. military effort to open the strait.

The UAE, by contrast, has lobbied Trump in recent days to take more decisive military action, with senior officials arguing that Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps won't compromise until the U.S. escalates, takes control of the strait, and perhaps considers ground operations, according to the Wall Street Journal.

Gulf Arab states had warned Trump directly that U.S. strikes on Iran's power plants would trigger Iranian retaliation against their own energy and desalination facilities, Reuters reported. Iran sent its own warning to Gulf capitals via an intermediary: any U.S. strike on Iranian power plants would "unleash unlimited retaliation."

The Diaspora Dimension

For the Indian diaspora, the stakes are enormous. The Gulf states host an estimated eight million Indian workers, and the Strait of Hormuz's effective closure since the war began has disrupted remittance flows and driven up fuel costs across South Asia. India, one of the world's largest oil importers, has faced persistent inflationary pressure from elevated crude prices. Any further escalation threatens the livelihoods of millions of Indian nationals in the Gulf region and the broader economic stability of their families back home.

What's Next

The war the U.S. and Israel launched on February 28 has now stretched past five months, with attacks spreading from the Gulf to the Red Sea and even the Mediterranean. An April ceasefire collapsed last month, sending Brent crude up 24%. Analysts polled by Reuters expect further price increases this year.

Trump faces mounting political pressure. Polling shows the Iran war is deeply unpopular in the U.S. and a drag on Republican midterm election hopes in November. Tehran is aware of this vulnerability — an Iranian diplomat told the Wall Street Journal that should diplomacy fail, the IRGC is considering pre-emptive strikes even without a U.S. attack.

"With or without an agreement, and regardless of any external commitments, if Iran attempts to renew its nuclear programme or advance its ballistic missile industries, we will be there. We will take action, and we will strike."

— Eli Cohen, Israel's Energy Minister

Trump said at a cabinet meeting Friday that he believed his negotiating team — including son-in-law Jared Kushner, special envoy Steve Witkoff, and Secretary of State Marco Rubio — could reach a deal. But with Iran's Houthi allies in Yemen now threatening the Bab el-Mandeb strait at the other end of the Red Sea, the window for diplomacy may be narrowing.
